title: Project offices: PMO types and their benefits
blurb: Tell embedded, central and hub-and-spoke PMOs apart, list what a PMO does, and explain the benefits it brings to governance.
question: An insurer runs 40 projects and three large programmes. Each programme has its own support team, but every project reports in a different format and lessons are never shared. What kinds of project office could it set up, what would they do, and what would the organisation gain?

teach.h: The project office: governance's support team
teach.body: A project, programme or portfolio management office (PMO, or P3O when all three are covered) is an organisational function that supports the delivery of projects and programmes and the management of the portfolio. It provides standards, methods, tools, reporting, planning support and assurance, and builds capability. Plain English: the PMO is the support team that helps projects run the same good way and makes sure decision-makers get reliable information. It supports governance; it does not replace the sponsor or project manager.

teach.h: Three ways to set up a PMO

teach.caption: The hub keeps everyone consistent; the spokes, embedded in programmes or business units, give hands-on help.

teach.body: Four benefits. CONSISTENCY: projects use the same methods and report the same way, so they can be compared. BETTER DECISIONS: sponsors, boards and portfolio managers get reliable, consolidated information. EFFICIENCY: shared tools, templates and expertise mean each project does not reinvent the wheel, and scarce people are used where they matter most. CAPABILITY BUILDING: training, coaching and shared lessons raise the organisation's project management maturity over time.

Each of Castlegate's three programmes had its own embedded office, but the 40 projects outside them reported in 40 formats. The insurer creates a hub-and-spoke PMO. The central hub sets one reporting template, a standard life cycle and a lessons library. The three programme offices become spokes, still giving hands-on planning help. Within a year the board sees one portfolio dashboard, data engineers are allocated by priority, and new PMs are trained on the same method.

A PMO supports governance; it does not own project decisions. The sponsor remains accountable for the business case and benefits, and the project manager for managing delivery. A PMO's assurance checks are valuable but come from inside the organisation's own functions, so they are not as independent as an external audit. Where teams work iteratively, a good PMO tailors its standards, for example accepting release-level reporting rather than forcing phase-gate documents on every time box.

teach.text: Exam traps: an EMBEDDED PMO sits inside one project or programme; a CENTRAL PMO serves the whole organisation; HUB-AND-SPOKE is both, a central hub with spokes in programmes or business units. And a PMO never 'takes over accountability' for delivery or benefits: those stay with the PM and sponsor.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name the PMO type and where it sits (embedded, central, hub-and-spoke).
Give two or three functions relevant to the scenario.
Link each to a benefit: consistency, better decisions, efficiency, capability.
Note the PMO supports governance; accountability stays with sponsor and PM.
PMO / P3O: a function supporting projects, programmes and the portfolio.
Embedded: inside one project or programme. Central: organisation-wide.
Hub-and-spoke: central hub sets standards; spokes give local support.
Functions: standards, reporting, planning, assurance, resources, knowledge, training.
Benefits: consistency, better decisions, efficiency, capability building.

summary: You can now describe embedded, central and hub-and-spoke PMOs, list the functions a PMO provides and explain the benefits it brings. You can also explain why a PMO supports governance without taking accountability away from the sponsor or project manager.

A.q: A support team sits inside a single large transport programme and serves only that programme. Which type of PMO is this?
A.why: An embedded PMO sits within, and serves, a single project or programme.

whyNot.0: A central PMO serves the whole organisation.
whyNot.2: Hub-and-spoke combines a central hub with several spokes; this is one standalone office.
whyNot.3: A portfolio board is a decision-making body, not a support office.

A.q: Which of the following is a typical PMO function?
A.why: Providing standards, methods and tools is a core PMO function.

whyNot.0: The sponsor owns the business case.
whyNot.1: Gate decisions are taken by the sponsor and board; a PMO may support the review.
whyNot.3: Users (or the product owner) accept outputs.

A.q: Which BEST describes a hub-and-spoke PMO?
options: One office inside a single project
Separate offices with no shared rules
A board that approves all spending
A central hub with local spokes
A.why: A central hub sets standards, methods and tools while spokes embedded in programmes or business units give local support.

whyNot.0: One office inside a single project is an embedded PMO.
whyNot.1: The hub exists precisely to give the spokes shared standards.
whyNot.2: A PMO supports governance; it is not a spending approval board.

B.q: A manufacturer replaces its many separate project support teams with one central PMO. What is the MAIN benefit it should expect?
options: Sponsors no longer need to be named
Regulations no longer apply to projects
B.why: A central PMO gives organisation-wide standards and a single view of all projects, improving consistency and decisions.

whyNot.1: Every project still needs a sponsor.
whyNot.2: A PMO supports PMs; it does not remove their authority.
whyNot.3: Regulations apply regardless of how a PMO is organised.

B.q: A council's projects keep repeating the same supplier mistakes because nobody records or shares what went wrong before. Which PMO function MOST directly addresses this?
B.why: Knowledge management captures lessons learned and makes them available to future projects.

whyNot.0: Resource management allocates people; it doesn't capture lessons.
whyNot.1: Planning support helps build schedules, not share past lessons.
whyNot.2: Training and coaching build skills, but the gap here is capturing and sharing lessons.

B.q: A central PMO now produces every project's monthly dashboard. Which statement is correct?
options: The PMO is now accountable for benefits
The PMO now chairs each project board
The PMO supports; decisions stay put
The PMO now manages each project team
B.why: The PMO supports governance with information; the sponsor stays accountable for the business case and the PM for managing delivery.

whyNot.0: Benefits accountability stays with the sponsor.

C.q: A global engineering firm wants every project to use the same methods and reporting, but its large programmes also need hands-on, local planning support. Which PMO model fits BEST?
C.why: Hub-and-spoke gives consistent standards from a central hub and local support through spokes in the programmes.

whyNot.1: Embedded offices alone would give local help but no shared standards.
whyNot.2: Without a PMO there is nothing to provide either the standards or the support.
whyNot.3: A central PMO alone gives standards but may be too remote for hands-on local help.

C.q: Four projects in a software company all need the same two data engineers in the same month. Which PMO function MOST helps?
C.why: Resource management gives a view across projects and helps allocate scarce people according to priority.

whyNot.0: Lessons won't resolve a live clash over scarce people.
whyNot.2: Standards make projects consistent but don't allocate people.
whyNot.3: Training builds skills over time; it won't solve this month's clash.

C.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical benefit of a PMO?
C.why: A PMO supports governance but never takes over the sponsor's accountability for benefits.

whyNot.0: Consistency is a core PMO benefit.
whyNot.1: Better decisions from reliable information is a core PMO benefit.
whyNot.2: Capability building through training and lessons is a core PMO benefit.

reteach.title: A chain of restaurants
reteach.question: A restaurant chain wants every branch to cook the same dishes to the same standard, but each kitchen needs its own help on busy nights. How is that like a PMO?

blocks.body: Head office writes the recipes, chooses the suppliers, trains new chefs and collects every branch's figures: that is a central PMO. A senior chef based in one flagship kitchen, helping only that kitchen, is an embedded office. Head office plus a roving senior chef in each region is hub-and-spoke. None of them owns the branch's results: each branch manager is still in charge of their own kitchen.

blocks.text: Head office makes branches consistent and better informed. It does not cook the dinners or take the blame for a bad night: that stays with the branch manager, just as delivery stays with the PM.

explain.body: Embedded: inside one project or programme, closing when it ends. Central: one office serving the whole organisation. Hub-and-spoke: a central hub setting standards, with spokes embedded in programmes or business units.

test.q: Which PMO type normally closes when the project or programme it serves ends?
test.why: An embedded PMO exists to support one project or programme, so it closes when that work ends.

whyNot.0: A central PMO is a permanent organisational function.
whyNot.1: A portfolio office supports the ongoing portfolio, so it is permanent.
whyNot.3: The hub of a hub-and-spoke PMO is permanent.

explain.body: Standards, methods and tools; reporting and information; planning support; assurance; resource management; knowledge management; and training. Each makes projects more consistent and better informed.

test.q: Which PMO function involves checking that projects follow agreed standards and are healthy?
test.why: PMO assurance checks compliance with standards and project health, giving confidence to decision-makers.

whyNot.0: Training builds skills; it doesn't check compliance.
whyNot.2: Planning support helps build plans, not check compliance.
whyNot.3: Resource management allocates people across projects.

explain.body: Consistency of methods and reporting; better decisions from reliable information; efficiency through shared tools and expertise; and capability building through training, coaching and shared lessons.

test.q: A PMO runs coaching sessions and a mentoring scheme for new project managers. Which benefit does this MOST directly deliver?
test.why: Training, coaching and mentoring raise the organisation's project management capability.

whyNot.1: No PMO activity exempts an organisation from regulation.
whyNot.2: Every project still needs a sponsor.
whyNot.3: Contract pricing is a procurement decision, not a PMO benefit.

explain.body: A project office supports one project; a programme office supports one programme's projects and benefits; a portfolio office supports the organisation in selecting, prioritising and balancing all its projects and programmes.

test.q: Which office supports selecting and prioritising projects across the whole organisation?
test.why: The portfolio office supports portfolio management: selecting, prioritising and balancing all the organisation's projects and programmes.

whyNot.0: A project office supports a single project.
whyNot.2: A programme office supports one programme.
whyNot.3: An embedded office sits within a single project or programme.
